chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad from Salih ibn Abi Hammad, raising it, said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) came to Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays to console him for the death of a brother of his named Abdul Rahman. So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you were to be impatient, you would have fulfilled the right of the womb (kinship), and if you were to be patient, you would have fulfilled the right of Allah. Indeed, if you are patient, the decree is executed upon you and you are praised; and if you are impatient, the decree is executed upon you and you are blamed.'

Al-Ash'ath said to him: 'Indeed we are to Allah and indeed to Him we are returning.' So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you know its interpretation?' Al-Ash'ath said: 'No. You are the peak and limit of knowledge.' He said to him: 'As for your saying 'Indeed we are to Allah', it is your acknowledgment of the Sovereignty. And as for your saying 'and to Him we are returning', it is your acknowledgment of the destruction/death.'
ai.seo_question: What is the deeper interpretation of 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Kafi, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) consoles Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays by distinguishing between the social duty of kinship fulfilled through grief and the spiritual duty to Allah fulfilled through patience. He further elucidates the theological depth of the phrase 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un', interpreting the first part as an acknowledgment of divine sovereignty (Al-Mulk) and the second as an admission of mortality and return to the Creator. This highlights the Shia emphasis on conscious, theological reflection during moments of personal loss.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Muhammad, from Salih Bin Abu Hammad, raising it, said,

‘Amir Al-Momineen came over to Al-Ash’as Bin Qays consoling him for (the demise of) a brother of his called Abdul Rahman. So Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘If you were to panic, you would have given the right of the womb (relationship), and if you were to be patient, so you would have paid the Right of Allah<sup>azwj</sup>. On top of that, if you were to be patient, the Ordained matter would flow upon you and you would be a praised one, and if you were to panic, the Ordained matter would flow upon you (anyway) and you would be a condemned one’.

So Al-Ash’as said to himasws, ‘[2:156] Surely we are for Allah and to Him we are returning;. So Amir Al-Momineenasws said: ‘Do you know what its interpretation is?’ So Al-Ash’as said, ‘No. Youasws are the peak of knowledge and its limit’. So heasws said to him: ‘We are for Allah – so it is the acknowledgement from you of the King. And as for your words and to Him we are returning – so it is the acknowledgement from you of the death’.
en.sarwar: 40. Ali ibn Muhammad has narrated from Salih ibn abu Hammad in a marfu‘ manner has said the following: “

’Amir al-Mu’minin, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, once visited Ash‘ath ibn Qays to offer condolences for the death of his brother, called, ‘Abd al-Rahman. ’Amir al-Mu’minin told him, ‘If you express grief, you have observed the right of relatives; but if you exercise patience you have observed the right of Allah. If you exercise patience, you cannot escape destiny but you will be praised, and if you express grief, still you cannot escape destiny but you will be blamed.’

Ash‘ath then said to him, ‘We are for Allah and to Him we return.’ ’Amir al-Mu’minin then asked, ‘Do you know what its explanation is?’ Ash‘ath replied, ‘No, you are the end and limit of knowledge.’ The Imam said, ‘Your saying, “we are for Allah,” is your professing that you are owned (by Allah) and your saying, “to Him we return”, is your professing to die.’”
